title: How a world-leading health study in a small town helped shape modern medicine
text:
Sixty years ago, regional West Australian GP Kevin Cullen had a brainwave.

Dr Cullen asked his patients in the West Australian regional community of Busselton, 220 kilometres south of Perth, if they would agree to be measured, tested, and followed over the course of their lives — all in the name of science.

The response rate was astounding. More than 90 per cent of Busselton's then-4,000 adult residents agreed to take part, unaware their commitment would eventually shape modern medicine.

Caravans, fitted out with medical gear, were set up across Busselton, where nurses and doctors tested the participants.

"We wanted to see whether mortality would decline, and [what we found] was something that was most exciting," he told the ABC in the 1980s.

Dr Kevin Cullen began the Busselton Health Study in 1966, pioneering the importance of preventative medicine. (ABC News)

Since its inception in 1966, the Busselton Health Study has collected data from more than 20,000 participants and has published 500 scientific papers.

The findings have helped to shape clinical guidelines around the globe for life-threatening conditions including heart disease, sleep apnoea, diabetes and asthma.

One of the world's longest-running population health studies, it has now returned to the regional city with an interactive mobile caravan installation to celebrate 60 years of lifesaving work.

In 1966 the study was conducted out of a series of caravans equipped with medical equipment. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Lifesaving discoveries

In exchange for their time, participants receive medical tests valued at up to $5,000, which can include blood, respiratory, cardiovascular and cognitive testing.

For some, the positive impacts of one of the world's longest-running human studies hit close to home.

Dawn Townsend was motivated to start volunteering for the study after it saved her husband's life.

"[The researchers] discovered that he had a 70 per cent blockage in one of his arteries," she said.

"It was something that he had seen in men who were fit and healthy who dropped dead on the doorstep.

"He's very happy to have gone to the study, found out what it is, and he's very healthy now."

Between them, Dawn Townsend (left) and Jean Chant have completed more than 22 years of volunteering with the study. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Her friend, Jean Chant, has volunteered for more than 20 years.

Ms Chant's favourite part of the study has been the connections she's made along the way.

"It's lovely when I ring them, and they say 'oh yes, good, I'd love to come in. When can I come?'" she said.

" It's just the attitude around town that really sticks with me, just how fond people are of the study. "

But as Busselton has evolved from a sleepy town to a thriving regional city, convincing new residents to sign up has been challenging.

Busselton residents queue at a survey caravan waiting for their tests in 1966. (Supplied: Busselton Population Medical Research Institute)

"Some of the newcomers to town aren't quite so familiar with it," she said.

"They need a bit of gentle persuasion."

Hopes for a further 60 years

Dr Cullen believed study participants should be informed of their results during testing, a change from the usual research model.

Busselton Population Medical Research Institute (BPMRI) director Michael Hunter said Dr Cullen's maverick approach to the research changed the script for health studies around the world.

"There was some pushback from the medical fraternity in that era, that the Busselton survey might create a whole population of hypochondriacs," he said.

"He firmly believed in preventative health medicine, and he was at the forefront of that concept."

One of a fleet of caravans which travelled to Busselton for testing. (Supplied: Busselton Population Medical Research Institute)

To celebrate six decades of research, the BPMRI has converted a caravan into a mobile exhibit, featuring archival photographs, footage and medical apparatus.

Associate Professor Hunter said he hoped the installation in Busselton's city centre would help entice more participants to the study.

"We want to inspire the next generation of participants and people to be involved," he said.

The installation is free and open to the public in Busselton's city centre and is offering free health checks to visitors. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Honouring those in need

Brian Moxham joined the study to honour his late first wife, whose battle with cancer involved experimental treatments only available to her through research projects like this one.

"With immunotherapy coming through, [my wife] was one of the first people to try that," he said.

"I think it's very important that if any one of us around here can still contribute in some way to any sort of health aspects to pass on to the health experts … that's how we're going to sort [sickness] out."

Brian Moxham and Christina Park joined the study later in life. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Christina Park said contributing to the study had the added benefit of giving her peace of mind when it came to her own wellbeing.

"I learned a lot about myself and my health," she said.

"Going to a doctor is a little bit different, but I think with the aging study, they took more time with me so I was able to get more benefit out of it."

The study is now trying to track down the baby boomers from the first cohort in 1966.

title: Origin Energy confirms some customers' bank account details accessed in hack
text:
Origin Energy has announced that as many as 60 customers had their full bank account numbers accessed by a hacker in July.

Last month, Origin confirmed a major cybersecurity breach affecting approximately 900,000 current and former customers.

The company has also updated the public, saying that for those 900,000 customers affected by the July security breach, information accessed included some combination of name, address, date of birth, contact phone number, account and other information about the customer's personal circumstances, as well as the last four digits of a credit card, or the last three digits of a bank account.

The hacker, Origin has confirmed, also accessed "numbers associated with government concession scheme or program, affecting approximately 15,000 customers in total".

The criminal investigation into the breach is still ongoing, Origin Energy CEO Frank Calabria said.

"We have substantially completed our review into the information accessed for each affected customer, and our priority is completing our notifications to them and providing support," he said in a statement.

" We have taken several steps to enhance the security of our systems to prevent future incidents of this kind. "

No customer data leaked publicly

The update from the energy company comes after authorities traced the cyber hack to a call centre in the Philippines, with the investigation linking the breach to a former Accenture employee in Manila.

Accenture works with Origin to run its call centres, but a spokesperson for the company declined to comment on the Origin incident when contacted by the ABC on Tuesday.

Origin Energy confirmed to the ABC that the alleged hacker had not leaked or disclosed any customer data to the public.

The breach was first reported by The Australian in July, when the alleged hacker sent a sample of 50 customer records containing names, addresses, emails, dates of birth, phone numbers and billing histories.

Only after The Australian sent that information to Origin Energy did the company alert authorities to a potential security breach.

The data breach is believed to be the largest known incident experienced by an Australian energy retailer. A cyber incident in September 2022 resulted in details of hundreds of EnergyAustralia customers being exposed.

Origin Energy customers had reported delays in receiving their energy bills in the days before the data breach was confirmed. However, the company said it was not connected to the incident.

Origin is one of several major Australian companies to experience a security breach, after Qantas suffered a major hack in 2025 and Optus and Medibank experienced breaches in 2022.

On Wednesday, Quest Apartment Hotels became the latest business to experience a security breach that affected customers' data.

title: Qantas, Virgin forced to BYO fuel to Fiji after 'very rare' contamination issue
text:
Airlines servicing Fiji are being forced to fly in fuel to the island nation as a fuel contamination issue hits the country's international airport.

Virgin Australia yesterday cancelled two services on its Fiji route and confirmed planes are being forced to stop halfway at airports such in New Caledonia and Vanuatu to make the journey back to Australia and Fiji.

In what one pilot described to the ABC as a "very rare" situation, airlines are being asked to fuel up at alternative airports if possible and bring in stockpiles of fuel to Nadi International Airport.

In correspondence seen by the ABC, pilots are being told that there is a "major contamination" and supply cannot be guaranteed in Fiji.

Pilots have been told the problem may continue until the end of the month.

One pilot said he has to bring in "more than 20 tonnes" of fuel to Fiji in order to make the flight back to Australia.

On a standard plane that services Fiji that equates to about one third to a quarter of a tank.

Qantas said it had switched to larger planes, a Boeing 737 to an Airbus A330, for the Sydney-Nadi route to avoid needing to refuel in Nadi.

Qantas said it had swapped to a larger Airbus 330 for the Sydney-Nadi flight. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Sources have told the ABC the contamination issue relates to an excessive electrical charge in a batch of fuel stored at the airport, however it was unclear where the issue originated from.

The source indicated it could be resolved soon or escalate into a more significant issue.

Fiji Airports did not confirm the cause of the contamination issue.

A spokesperson said they were making "operational adjustments" and the airport was "closely monitoring the current aviation fuel situation".

"Nadi International Airport remains open and operational, with established safety and operational protocols being maintained," it said.

Disability advocate removed from flight over wheelchair dispute Virgin Australia says it is reviewing an incident where a wheelchair user was removed from a flight after his battery-powered motor could not be stored in overhead lockers on board.

Virgin Airlines generally operates six flights a day to and from Fiji, from Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne. It cancelled two flights yesterday, one to Fiji from Brisbane and its returning flight.

According to tracking sites, flights so far today are scheduled to continue.

A Virgin spokesman described the contamination as a "temporary fuel issue".

"We understand more fuel has arrived into Nadi and is undergoing the standard testing and approval processes required before use," the spokesperson said.

Fiji faces fuel shock

Fiji Airlines is by far the most active in the country, operating about 80 domestic and international flights out of the airport per day.

Passengers vomiting as Fiji flight makes three landing attempts A Fiji Airways flight from Sydney had to divert after bad weather from a tropical cyclone thwarted its attempts to land.

The airline has been contracted for comment, however sources indicate it is working around the situation with its flights prioritised for refuelling.

This week, local media in Fiji reported the national airline was facing an $80 million surge in its fuel bill, putting further pressure on the airline's finances.

National Broacaster FBC reported the government approved an additional $127 million guarantee to help the national carrier manage rising fuel costs.

Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel said the increase was part of what the government describes as Fiji Airways' biggest fuel shock in more than 50 years.

title: Firmus AI data centre gets tick from planners ahead of council vote
text:
Council planners have recommended a controversial proposed artificial intelligence data centre in Tasmania's north be approved.

George Town Council will vote on Tuesday whether to approve Firmus Technologies's proposed 288-megawatt facility at Long Reach, at the old pulp mill site, in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone.

The planning application attracted 349 submissions from the public, while an electronic petition containing more than 5,000 signatures called on the council to reject it.

The council had extended the period where the public could make submissions, after complaints from nearby residents about a lack of community consultation.

The submissions detailed concerns including water and energy use; noise, air and light pollution; bushfire risk and environmental impact.

If approved, Firmus Technologies' proposed AI data centre will be built at the former Gunns Pulp Mill site near Bell Bay. (Supplied)

Council's planning officers responded to each of the concerns in the upcoming council meeting's published agenda, stating some of them were not factors regulated by the Tasmanian Planning Scheme.

"While many representations raise broader issues relating to energy policy, artificial intelligence, national security and Commonwealth regulation, these matters are either addressed through separate statutory frameworks or fall outside the scope of the planning authority's role in determining the application," they stated.

They recommended council approve the development, with conditions.

Firmus is currently building a 104-megawatt AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards, which is slated to begin operating early next year.

Firmus Technologies' construction of an AI data centre in St Leonards is underway. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

It has also submitted a development application for a 52-megawatt AI data centre in Wesley Vale, in the state's north-west.

The facilities will host data centre infrastructure and specialised computers which produce AI tokens, which are needed for AI tools such as chatbot ChatGPT.

The company is set to become the state's biggest power user if the three sites go ahead.

Project is 'wholly compliant' with planning scheme

A render of Firmus Technologies' proposed AI data centre at Long Reach, near George Town, taken from George Town Council meeting attachments in August 2026. (Supplied)

George Town Mayor Greg Kieser said council's decision-making role was limited to whether the development was compliant with the planning scheme.

"We have one decision to make: whether an application is consistent and compliant with the planning code — that's it," he told 936 ABC Hobart.

"I know there's a lot of interest on this topic, but policy is just purely not our remit."

He said the council's planning officers had assessed the development application according to the planning scheme.

George Town Council mayor Greg Kieser says the council must decide if the proposal is compliant with planning codes. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

"It would appear that they think that it is wholly compliant and as such their recommendation is to approve it," he said.

He said the public was welcome to attend Tuesday's council meeting, but warned "it can be a pretty dry affair".

Conditions attached to approval

The planning officers recommended the development's approval come with a number of conditions.

One was to update the bushfire plan and emergency management strategy, after Firmus incorrectly reported the number of diesel generators it planned to have on site.

Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis, the co-CEOs of Firmus Technologies, plan to build three data centres in northern Tasmania. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Officers also detailed conditions for the 276 backup diesel generators, which they said should only be operated during a failure or interruption of the mains electricity supply; for inspection, testing or maintenance; or in response to a genuine emergency.

Planning officers also said the simultaneous operation of more than one generator must not exceed a cumulative total of 24 hours in any given year.

They also recommended an updated noise emissions assessment — which "demonstrates that the operation of the development will comply with the noise criteria" — and for Firmus to undertake a noise verification survey within 60 days of commencing operation.

Furthermore, they said Firmus should keep a public complaints register, with records to be provided to the council's environmental health officer on request.

title: Once-secret son of Belgium royal becomes a prince at age 26
text:
The once-secret son of a Belgian royal has been legally recognised, becoming a prince at age 26.

Prince Laurent of Belgium reportedly established legal ties to his son, Clément Vandenkerckhove, at a town hall ceremony six months ago, although details have only just emerged.

While he formally becomes a prince, the former car salesman will not receive a royal allowance, the BBC reported.

The official recognition was first reported by Belgian weekly news magazine Soir Mag, which said the new prince would receive an equal share of his father's inheritance as a result of the legal change.

Mr Vandenkerckhove told the outlet he did not care for the law's technicalities, but rather the "chance to get to know his father".

Prince Laurent has three other children with his wife, Princess Claire of Belgium. (Reuters: Francois Lenoir)

The 26-year-old is the son of King Philippe's brother and model-singer Wendy Van Wanten.

His royal parentage has long been the subject of rumours.

Mr Vandenkerckhove — who was born in 2000 — bears a physical resemblance to Prince Laurent, his name has been interpreted as a reference to Prince Laurent's Tervuren home, Villa Clémentine, and Van Wanten had also dropped hints in her songs.

However, his existence was only recognised last year by Prince Laurent, who said the pair had "spoken openly and honestly about this in recent years".

Belgium's King Albert hands power over to son Philippe Belgium's King Albert has abdicated in favour of his son, Philippe, after 20 years on the throne.

At the age of 16, Mr Vandenkerckhove found out that Prince Laurent was his biological father.

He said he was 20 when he reached out to the prince.

"My entire childhood, I struggled with the question 'Who is my father?' When I found out, the secrecy weighed incredibly heavy," he told Flemish newspaper Het Nieuwsblad earlier this month.

" Imagine this: you know who your father is, but you aren't allowed to tell anyone. "

Mr Vandenkerckhove noted he was likely to keep his own surname rather than accept his father's name, Saxe-Coburg.

"Giving up this family name would be a betrayal of everything my mother has done for me," he added.

Prince Laurent has three other children with his wife, Princess Claire of Belgium, whom he married in 2003.

In 2020, his father, King Albert II, also recognised an illegitimate child after a long legal battle waged by now-Princess Delphine.

Albert II abdicated as king of the Belgians in 2013 as the paternity issue became a scandal.

title: Sweat and spectacle of theatre makes it 'immortal' but challenges lurk
text:
After four years touring in musicals across Australia and Asia, Jordan Koulos has found himself playing a deep-sea vampire spellbound by "a gothic, more seductive Atlantis".

"It's what happens under the surface that you never get to see, and being able to shock audiences with that," he said.

" It's this world you are just immersed in. "

Mr Koulos has forged a career in musical theatre, a $531 million sector that stretches from major stage shows to intimate cabaret.

"It's my bread and butter, I really love it," he said.

Jordan Koulos, seen here performing in Abyss at Dracula's, is enjoying his career in musical theatre. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

This latest role has brought Mr Koulos to Dracula's, a theatre-restaurant that has been entertaining audiences on the Gold Coast for 41 years.

But keeping the curtain up will not be easy.

'Dinner and a show'

Luke Newman's grandparents founded Dracula's Cabaret in 1985, inspired by the cult-classic Rocky Horror Picture Show and Vaudevillian theatre of the 19th century.

"People would go out to nightclubs where they'd have coffee at 11pm at night and watch a comedy act with a piano and ukulele on stage," he said.

"But nowadays, dinner and a show is nowhere else — it's very rare to see."

Dracula's was started by the Newman family on the Gold Coast in 1985. (Supplied: Dracula's)

Mr Newman started out "scraping plates" in Dracula's kitchen before working his way up to CEO.

"Dracula's operates in a bubble almost," he said.

"There's change coming, or it's already here with streaming and the way content is delivered."

Aerialist Ceejay Shuttleworth performs high above the audience. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

He said it takes a crew of 50 people to bring the production to stage five nights a week, with another show touring Australia and New Zealand for six months.

"Dracula's has bucked trends in the industry," he said.

"[But] it's a difficult time for live theatre and entertainment and we've heard lots of bad news stories about musicals closing and the impact that has on the industry and people advocating for support."

Once common, the idea of a dinner and a show has become rare. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Audiences are up, revenue is down

Several major theatrical productions touring Australia have recently been cancelled due to growing cost pressures.

Live Performance Australia's attendance report, published last year, found that while audience numbers were up, annual revenue fell 2 per cent to $531 million.

"That's consistent really nationally across all markets and genres of live performance," CEO Eric Lassen said.

"Everything from labour and technical costs to, for those shows that need to be touring around the country, the cost of freight has gone up well over 50 per cent."

The national tour of the musical Beetlejuice was cancelled in June due to cost pressures. (Supplied: Michael Cassel Group/Michelle Grace Hunder)

Mr Lassen said "the hunger and the demand" remains strong for live shows but increased costs put pressure on ticket prices.

"But producers are not able to raise ticket prices beyond a certain price point," he said.

"So they're operating at increasing risk and at increasingly slim margins to ensure they're actually going to recoup their costs."

Demand remains strong for live shows, but increased costs is putting pressure on ticket prices. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Mr Lassen has called for tax incentives to help producers offset the up-front costs of a new show.

"Building sets, designing costumes, workshopping everything that happens before the curtains rise," he said.

"The idea would be that a percentage of those costs, not the ongoing running costs, would be subject to an offset against future profits."

The federal government's consultation and development of a new National Cultural Policy is underway.

'Entertainment is immortal'

Mr Newman said he was confident Dracula's "stadium in a theatre" approach to entertainment will "thrive" through future challenges.

"What you can't substitute is live — live vocals, live guitar, people spinning from the roof above your head, sweat flying from their forehead," he said.

"You can feel it, you can taste it, you can touch it, and that's why this kind of entertainment is immortal."

Jordan Koulos, here as Finn in Dracula's production Abyss, says performing to a live audience is a wonderful feeling. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Jordan Koulos said musical theatre can "tease all the senses" in a way screens cannot.

"Coming from a musical theatre background, we see all the troubles the industry is facing, and we are semi in that," he said.

"[But] we see everyone that, even though they could be in the middle of a meal, they put their knife and fork down and just focus on you.

"It's just such a great feeling."

title: Swans captain 'deeply shocked' by scandal, denies player rift claims
text:
Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox and captain Callum Mills have addressed reporters amid the scandal that has engulfed the club this week.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" by the scandal and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

Dean Cox and Callum Mills addressed the media. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"As a playing group, we fully support the club's decisions on the sanctions handed down."

Mills said the five players would have to address the playing group, but there was no rift among the players.

Cox confirmed he was not in the room at the centre of the scandal, but would not be drawn on whether other staff members or players were present.

Both men refused to answer specific questions about the events that took place in the hotel room, saying they were the subject of a police investigation.

The Swans players and staff observed the press conference from behind the camera. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cox was also pressed on the club's decision to have the five suspended players driven back to Sydney from Melbourne, rather than flown. He said: "Decisions were made [as to] how we best support our players within the circumstances that happened."

Cox admitted the club's previously acclaimed culture had "taken a hit" as a result of the scandal.

"Our culture isn't perfect," he said.

"We going to work through as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been."

Live Moment Catch up up the key moments from Dean Cox and Callum Mills's press conference from Swans HQ. The press conference is over Dean Cox and Callum Mills have finished answering questions at Swans HQ. Cox's message to Sydney's fans ahead of the weekend Cox is asked what his message is to the club's fans considering coming to this weekend's games. "I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs. "We want to show that on Sunday." Is there concern for the mental health of the players? Mills is asked whether he is concerned for the mental health of the players suspended by the club. "There's concern in every part. That's the women in the community, our players involved, the women involved. "The wellbeing of everyone involved is [of] the utmost importance." Show more

Both Cox and Mills apologised to the club's AFLW team, with Mills saying he had addressed the group personally.

"I acknowledged their pain and I deeply apologised for the actions of a few within our group," he said.

Cox added that he hoped the supporters would still come out in force for the double-header at the SCG this weekend.

"I hope our fans stand by us and our club is united, our playing group is united, between both programs," he said.

"We want to show that on Sunday."

Sydney's men's team rounds out its home and away season with a clash against North Melbourne on Sunday afternoon at the SCG, a match preceded by an AFLW match between Sydney's women's team and Essendon's women's team at the same venue.

title: As costs rise and income falls, live music industry hopes to reverse decline
text:
A hundred years ago the Old Mount Gambier Gaol was home to the region's convicts and criminals.

Since its decommissioning in the 1990s it has become a hub for events, accommodation, and played host to some of the region's largest music shows.

Over the decade and a half James and Mel Stephenson have owned the Old Gaol they have brought in artists of a range of genres, from Hilltop Hoods to Missy Higgins to Jimmy Barnes.

But Mr Stephenson said these sorts of marquee shows, drawing as many as 5,000 people, are becoming more difficult to deliver.

"Everything's just gone up two, three, four or five times [in cost], that's the main difference from when we started to now," he said.

"It's not just the artists, it's toilets, it's security, it's logistics, it's front of house, it's staging.

Old Mount Gambier Gaol proprietor James Stephenson has received personal abuse for failing to secure gigs. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

"It makes it a bit hard, not just for myself but for the promoters and how much they want to get out of a show.

" They simply do the maths and go, 'It's too hard.' "

Not attracting shows has seen Mr Stephenson face some criticism online, including personal attacks from disappointed locals, prompting him to speak up on social media.

"The majority is positive because of the things that we do for Mount Gambier, but we also get the negative," he said.

"I understand that people can get frustrated simply because it's not here, but they don't understand the work to get things here."

Festivals at the Old Mount Gambier Gaol have drawn thousands. (Supplied: James Stephenson)

Nationwide post-COVID decline

The challenges facing the Old Gaol are not unique.

Across regional Australia, venues of varying sizes are struggling to provide a local music scene, as increased costs, declining alcohol sales and the lingering impacts of COVID continue.

"It's a very different thing to what it used to be like two or three decades ago when we had a significant and healthy live music scene," MusicSA CEO Christine Schloithe said.

"Behaviour patterns in live music venues have changed over time so it makes it difficult for live music venues to drive that profitable model that they are used to, based on alcohol sales.

"The cost of transport and fuel in vehicles to get artists around is really significant, as is the cost of insurance.

" There's a whole range of pressures, and what it's done is broken and fragmented the regional scene. "

Acts like Gernz are finding it harder to make a name for themselves as the number of shows decline. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Back in Mount Gambier, Liam Brown and his mates Bradley Frost and Kyle Gleed have spent several years playing in bands, currently performing as the rock band Gernz.

While they regularly play shows around the city, they've also performed on bigger shows with bands like Spiderbait and DZ Deathrays.

"It's one of the most exciting feelings when you've got people singing your music back at you," he said.

But over his time in the scene, he's seen the number of shows shrink.

"The opportunities are sliding," he said.

"It's harder for the venues to put on these events — it's very expensive."

Kylie Ind runs live shows at her brewery in Mount Gambier. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

The owners of the Woolstore Brewery, just across the road from the Gaol, are doing their best to expand the opportunities for local bands.

Kylie Ind said there were some challenges stepping up from smaller gigs to running their first festival this year.

"Going up a step into festivals, obviously the costs grow astronomically," she said.

"That's been a really hard balancing act to make it affordable for people.

"We want them to come and bring their family and bring their friends, but also make sure that we're reimbursing the people that are putting in their time and energy to perform."

Tours featuring well-known artists like Paul Kelly are getting harder to hold in regional areas. (Supplied: James Stephenson)

Investment, initiatives needed

With towns across the country looking to reverse the concerning trend, stakeholders will descend on Mount Gambier in October for a national regional music summit.

Ms Schloithe said MusicSA wants to highlight some of its efforts to bring life to the Limestone Coast's music scene.

"[There's been] 12 to 18 months worth of really solid work that MusicSA has been doing in the Mount Gambier region supporting venues to increase live music in their venues, and to support that touring corridor between Melbourne and Adelaide," she said.

" We've had such a great response. Music is starting to thrive in that region again. "

MusicSA CEO Christine Schloithe says efforts are being made in Mount Gambier to revive local music. (ABC News: Ben Pettit)

Mr Brown said it was vital regional music is kept alive, not just for artists and venues, but also for the public more broadly.

"If people don't have something to go to and attend where they feel welcomed by a group of people, that's when people start going left and really getting themselves into trouble," he said.

"Getting a venue like the Woolstore or the Globe [Hotel] or the Old Gaol putting those events on enables some of the best of the best to perform and people that are just starting out to perform, to get that new audience to work on their craft and try their best to get somewhere."

title: These workers were 'paid in rations' 60 years ago, so they walked off the job
text:
To Kalkarindji Gurindji traditional owner and elder Rob Roy, the Wave Hill Walk-Off is one of the most important turning points in Australian history, which ultimately returned his land, and more than half of the Northern Territory, to Aboriginal people.

"It's such a historic event because it changed Australia in regard to fair wages — it was one of those pivotal moments," Mr Roy said.

"Vincent Lingiari fought against all the odds, and so his legacy will remain hundreds of years from now; he literally changed the whole nation of Australia."

Rob Roy says the Wave Hill Walk-Off changed Australia. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

This weekend, hundreds of people will converge on the remote community of Kalkarindji to celebrate the 60th anniversary of Gurindji leader Vincent Lingiari leading 200 Indigenous cattlemen and domestic servants off the station, in strike action over their employer Vestey Brothers' refusal to pay them wages equal to non-Indigenous workers.

From the Wave Hill protest to land handbacks Vincent Lingiari led 200 stockmen and house workers to walk off the job at the Wave Hill cattle station. This timeline looks back at the key events, before and after that historic day.

It came after the Commonwealth Conciliation and Arbitration Commission had in March 1966 ruled Indigenous cattle station workers should no longer suffer wage discrimination, but that change would not happen for three years.

The Gurindji workers' refusal to accept that delay, and anger over the cattle station operator's unwillingness to recognise their traditional ownership of the land, led to a political struggle that prompted then-prime minister Gough Whitlam in 1972 to commit to "establish once and for all Aborigines' rights to land".

In 1975, Mr Whitlam ceremonially poured soil from Mr Lingiari's country into his hands, and in 1976 the federal government passed the Land Rights Act, allowing NT traditional owners to start re-establishing their land ownership through the courts.

Gough Whitlam pouring soil into the hands of Vincent Lingiari, symbolically handing the station back in 1975. (AGNSW: Mervyn Bishop)

Mr Roy said his father Roy was a stockman on Wave Hill and his mother Maryanne was a domestic servant to the station manager, and both parents took part in the walk-off.

"My parents told me they walked away from the living conditions," he said.

"It was pretty hard, all they had was tin sheds to cover up from the rain and heat and cold.

"They got paid in rations, like flour, sugar and tea; there were no proper wages.

"The old fella Vincent Lingiari told everyone to gather round, and he said, 'We've had enough, we're going to go, we're going to walk.'

" How they were treated, he wanted to break away from that; he wanted to take his people away so they could do things on their own their way, on their own land. "

He said the group who walked off didn't realise their strike would evolve into a full-blown political battle to have their land rights recognised.

Rob Roy says Vincent Lingiari's legacy will continue for hundreds of years. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

But Mr Roy said even now, there was still a lot more work to be done to ensure Indigenous communities that have had their land rights recognised are benefiting financially and socially.

"A lot of the communities in the Territory, and Australia, we're still struggling in regard to medical, housing, education — there's a little bit more fight left over," he said.

Across the NT, the recognition of land rights has meant more than $3 billion in royalties has been paid to traditional owners, their representative land councils and an economic and community development fund, by governments and companies.

The money comes from traditional owners hosting mines, railway lines, pipelines and other infrastructure on their land.

But Mr Roy said he wanted to see more young Indigenous people working on their land.

"A lot of the communities try — we have our own businesses, including the community shop here," he said.

"I wouldn't say we're that successful yet but then there's also success in self-determination."

Speed of change brought 'devastating' results

John Mills, pictured as a young man, was an overseer at Wave Hill when the walk-off occurred. (Supplied: John Mills)

In the early 1970s, John Mills was an overseer and relief manager on Wave Hill Station.

To him, the legacy of the Wave Hill Walk-Off is high levels of Indigenous unemployment across the Territory, many communities reliant on government welfare and royalties, and with high levels of alcohol-related health and social problems.

"To me, it was devastating — people went to settlements like Kalkarindji, they lost a lot of purpose in their lives and a lot of their culture, partly because of alcohol, and money they didn't know what to do with," he said.

Employment statistics from the 2021 census show Indigenous employment in remote Australia is only 42 per cent.

Mr Mills said before the walk-off, a majority of their workers were Indigenous.

"Most of the people on the station were gainfully employed, and their families lived in a camp on the station," he said.

"The station also provided medical, a school, and all the food [was] supplied by the station.

"I can't remember the dollar figure that they got paid, but it wasn't much; being clothed and fed was part of it."

John Mills says cattle station workers and their families had been living at Wave Hill before the walk-off. (Supplied: John Mills)

He said in the years after the walk-off, the station had fewer Indigenous staff — a situation that was mirrored around the Territory.

John Mills says the cattle station was left short-staffed after the walk-off. (Supplied: John Mills)

"After the walk-off, we were fairly short-staffed — we employed more white jackaroos and more fencing went up so we didn't need as many people," Mr Mills said.

"The camp was closed down because we couldn't afford to pay the Aboriginal staff the going wages and keep them as well.

"They got paid what they should, and the older people got their pensions.

"To me, for some people getting that money was their downfall.

"Wave Hill was a dry station, but we had difficulty keeping people there because as soon as they got paid, they went off to Top Springs to buy grog.

" I'm not saying things shouldn't have changed, but it needed to have been done in a slower, more organised way. "

Hopes for more Indigenous station workers

From 2008, the NT Cattlemen's Association (NTCA) tried for almost two decades to get more Indigenous people back working on stations through a Pastoral Real Jobs Program that it ran with the Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation.

But a few years ago the corporation cut the funding, telling the ABC it had focused its "investment where it delivers the greatest benefit to Indigenous-held land and Indigenous-owned and controlled organisations".

The NT Cattlemen's Association runs the Pastoral Real Jobs Program to encourage more Aboriginal people to take up work in the industry. (Suppled: NT Cattlemen's Association)

NTCA president Romy Carey said the association was hoping to attract funding from the federal or NT governments that would allow it to restart the jobs program.

"We were providing accredited training and pathways for jobs on cattle stations, or if people decided cattle work wasn't for them, assisting them with a pathway into other work like civil construction," she said.

"It was very beneficial for the industry because a workforce can be very hard to find and retain in our regional areas, and it was beneficial for our communities who were able to source work close to home and close to country.

"It is a priority for our membership and our directors to identify opportunities for us to have that program funded again."

The Pastoral Real Jobs Program had been run in conjunction with the Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation, but funding has since been cut. (Supplied: NT Cattlemen's Association)

In Kalkarindji, Mr Roy said he was happy to see growing numbers of young people, including his niece, working on their country as rangers, managing weeds, feral animals and conservation.

But he said he wanted the legacy of the Wave Hill Walk-Off to be more young people in work.

"We're pushing for kids to get a better education, whether they want to run a business or get a job, to benefit themselves, and get a sense of responsibility for looking after the community," he said.

title: Bugs bassist Jordan Brunoli approaching final months of life
text:
It's difficult to comprehend the intensity of Jordan Brunoli's past week.

Over just a few days the bassist from Brisbane band Bugs has celebrated his wedding, prepared for the upcoming release of Bugs's first album in years, and taken a call from his oncologist who explained what he might expect in his final days of life.

"We were planning the wedding and planning a funeral at the same time," he tells triple j hack.

"How insane is that?"

Loading...

Jordan's announcement last year that he had been diagnosed with stage 4 colorectal cancer devastated the Australian music community.

On Sunday, he shared an update on social media, confirming his cancer had continued to spread and he was told in June that he was entering the final chapter of life, with "a prognosis of 3–4 months".

" My oncologist says: 'The chemo is not working at all anymore and it's looking like we might have to start referring you to palliative care.' "

While he acknowledges the bad news did not come as a surprise, the 30-year-old says it still doesn't feel real.

"Those who've seen me recently have just gone 'what the hell man, you look fine.'

"It feels like a dream … like I'm talking about someone else.

"I still want to keep living life … and every day I'm just trying to do more."

'It's just acceptance'

Jordan admits the last year has been an emotional rollercoaster.

"I had a terrible couple of months … I was super depressed, became very inward.

"I shrunk my circle, not deliberately, but my inner circle became very small, and I stopped responding to people like my close friends as well."

Loading Instagram content

But recently, Jordan says he's noticed a shift.

"There's this weird Gandhi-ness about me, I've been told!

"I think it's just acceptance.

"I've just accepted what's going to happen, and there's nothing that can change."

The Bugs bond

Coming to terms with Jordan's future has also been difficult for Bugs bandmates Connor Brooker and Brock Weston.

"We've had hard conversations," Connor admits.

" But we're kind of trying to avoid focusing on it too much because I think there's too much we still want to achieve together. "

That includes releasing the Bugs' first album in years, Head Noise, which comes out next Friday.

"It's about damn time," Jordan says.

"We've been working on it for a very long time, and we've had a bit of a catalyst that's forced us to get it out.

"Let's go, because we don't have any time."

Bugs will perform two shows at Brisbane venue Crowbar, formerly The Zoo, in September to launch their new album, Head Noise. (Supplied: Will Johnstone)

Brock says Head Noise pushes Bugs into different directions.

"We got to really curate the whole album into a new sound and the result is amazing," he tells hack.

The band has also announced two shows in Brisbane early next month.

"I'll be playing the gigs, even if I'm crawling on stage and crawling off," Jordan stresses.

"We have a contingency hologram just in case!" Connor jokes.

Picking out the casket

Jordan admits the seriousness of the situation sometimes makes for some "hilariously depressing" moments.

He explains how invaluable his partner, George, has been, as she navigates keeping him focused while planning his funeral.

Jordan Brunoli says his partner, Georgia, and bandmates Brock (right) and Connor have been great supports as he navigates the last few months of his life. (triple j: Brandon Lung)

"Sometimes I'll just be sitting on the couch hanging out with the dogs and all of a sudden G [George] hits me with a 'Hey, which one of these caskets do you want to be buried in?'"

"Seriously, though, if I didn't have Brock, Connor and my partner, G, keeping me grounded every day … I wouldn't be anywhere near as comfortable as I am right now.

"G and I were meant to be and always will be."

Jordan and George celebrated their wedding with loved ones yesterday.

'The reason we're still here'

The huge wave of support and love that has poured in for Jordan over the past week from Bugs fans is not lost on him.

"You guys are freaking legends, and we love you so much," he says.

"To have them come along with you for the ride for 10 years … that's amazing.

"It's the people who have supported us that's the reason we're still here."

Loading Instagram content

Connor interjects with his own thoughts on why Bugs fans have been so loyal.

"I think the reason why a lot of them have supported us is because of you, Jordan.

"You invest so much into fans, listening to them, making moments with them.

"I'm really proud to have been able to do that with you because you light up a room."

The trio laugh as they consider the cliches they are throwing at each other, but it's clear the love and respect runs deep.

"We've always been the kind of dudes that have hugged each other goodbye and say I love you," Connor says.

"Jordan is so tough," Brock adds.

"As a friend, I've just tried to focus on not doing anything different."

'The fighter in me'

Jordan says he is doing his best to prepare for death, but is also very much focused on living right now.

" No I'm not ready, but you know what? I don't think that fact is ever going to change. "

He says his predominant emotion is fear — not of dying, but of not making the most of the time he has left.

A lot of his time, he says, is spent considering how his loved ones will cope once he's gone.

Jordan Brunoli says young people shouldn't be so hard on themselves and everyone should go to therapy. (triple j: Brandon Lung)

Not much of his time is spent on thinking about how he'll be remembered.

"I don't actually give a f***!" he laughs.

But he does have advice for young Australians on how they might approach life.

"I don't think there's a secret formula, but the only thing I will say is, don't be so hard on yourself.

"And go to therapy!"

However the end plays out, Jordan says he will confront it head on.

"There's that fighter in me, you know?

"I have a feeling I'm just going to push till the end."

title: Rise in Kimberley animal abuse cases linked to cost of living
text:
Mounting financial pressures are leading to an increase in animal cruelty reports, according to the RSPCA, with the problem especially acute in Western Australia's far north.

WARNING: This story contains images of an emaciated animal and animal neglect readers may find distressing.

The organisation said cases of animal abuse in the Kimberley had risen 23 per cent in the past financial year, and it had doubled its intake of animals from the region.

RSPCA WA spokesperson Louise Rowe said in many cases, the neglect appeared to stem from cost-of-living strains.

There has been a rise in the number of malnourished, neglected animals in the Kimberley. (Supplied: RSPCA )

"We're seeing really emaciated animals because they're not being fed enough. We're seeing animals with chronic skin conditions because they're not getting parasite treatments," she said.

" We're seeing animals suffering from ailments that really could have been fixed a lot sooner if they received proper medical care. "

The increase has prompted the charity to provide community outreach days in Broome and Derby, offering free pet health checks, microchipping, pet food and flea and worm treatments.

'No excuse'

There are "undoubtedly" more cases of abuse happening across the Kimberley that the charity does not know about, Ms Rowe said.

She said RSPCA relied on the community to be its "eyes and ears" and urged people who had animal welfare concerns to reach out.

"We know people are struggling. We know that times are tough, but that's no excuse to let your animals suffer," Ms Rowe said.

"Animals should be cared for. They can't do it for themselves, and owners have a responsibility to reach out sooner rather than later."

The RSPCA urged the community to report instances of animal abuse. (Supplied: RSPCA )

RSPCA WA appointed an inspector in the Kimberley in 2022 after the region recorded some of the highest animal cruelty in the state.

But the role was scrapped when it became apparent the lone inspector's safety was at risk.

"We've introduced a fly-in, fly-out model, which is working really well," Ms Rowe said.

"If we get a report that needs urgent action, we can attend ourselves, or we work with others in the area as well that can help us on the ground."

Charities overrun

Saving Animals From Euthanasia (SAFE) Broome is the only animal rescue organisation in town.

Coordinator Sonya Debenham said the biggest challenge was finding foster homes.

Sonya Debenham says vet bills for the animals can cost between $10,000 and $15,000 a month. (Supplied: SAFE)

This challenge has only been compounded by the noticeable increase of cats and dogs coming into their care.

"The strays and wandering dogs is about the same, but really abandonment and surrenders are higher because the cost of living has gone up so much," Ms Debenham said.

" People are struggling to support the pets they've got. "

Ms Debenham said there could be 70 to 120 animals at SAFE at any time.

Anyone who comes across an injured or abused animal is urged to contact the RSPCA on 1300 CRUELTY or 1300 278 358.

title: The healthcare change that has some veterans furious
text:
In the Senate on Wednesday, Jacqui Lambie rose to speak on an extraordinarily personal topic — her recent surgery for vaginal prolapse.

She told the parliament of her challenges in seeking the surgery through the Department of Veterans Affairs (DVA), and her eventual decision to pay for the surgery out of her own pocket.

"If I was like the majority of female veterans, I would have had to wait for DVA to approve my claim," she said.

"And then I would have to search, and hope, and hope, that there would be a gynaecologist that would accept the low rate paid by DVA.

"That's how much they care about our vaginas."

Senator Lambie was visibly emotional when she described her health challenges. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She linked her personal experience to the concerns being expressed by other veterans about looming changes to how the DVA manages access to allied healthcare.

From the middle of next year, a $5,000 threshold will be introduced for veterans spending on allied healthcare.

The government is quick to point out that it is not a cap. But spending over $5,000 will be subject to new scrutiny to determine if it is "clinically effective".

Senator Lambie's specific situation was not related to the changes, but she said the threshold could have harmed her ability to seek physiotherapy post-surgery.

Matt Keogh says he wants little real-world impact on veterans as a result of the changes. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The government is now facing substantial pressure over its plans, and was not helped when Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh told the parliament he "got it wrong" after initially declining a meeting with veterans concerned about the threshold.

Government sources suggest questions around the threshold are being considered at the highest levels, including up to the prime minister's office.

What's changing?

The $5,000 threshold was first announced in May's budget.

It was described as an "annual monetary limit for veterans' allied health services" that would save the budget roughly $750 million over three years and $340 million each year after that.

The threshold aims to limit what the government describes as "overservicing" — where there is no clinical justification for the volume of appointments and services provided.

Veterans have access to various healthcare benefits covered by the government, including allied health care depending on injuries or conditions resulting from their service.

NT veterans join calls for health funding cap removal The federal government wants to cap access to health supports to $5,000 a year for injured war veterans, but there are growing concerns some will be worse-off as a result.

Department figures suggest that only around 10 per cent of veteran cardholders spend more than $5,000 on allied health services each year.

A Senate estimates hearing in June heard examples of overcharging that the department said it was keen to tackle.

In one case, a single patient was charged $101,000 in a single year by a dietitian, equating to 19 appointments a week.

Another veteran was charged $47,000 in a year for podiatry.

Department officials pointed to these as extreme examples of what it considered to be overservicing.

Its answer is the $5,000 threshold — granting funds to that amount but charges beyond would be subject to a "demonstrated clinical need".

Finding a fix

Both the department and minister, Matt Keogh, have pointed to a long period of planned consultation to run before the changes take effect.

There is a stated desire to ensure there is no service gap — that is, when veterans hit the $5,000 threshold they are not barred from accessing services they need while paperwork is processed.

But exactly how that will work is not yet clear.

The government has pointed to its process of consultation as its means of working out answers to questions like how clinical need will be measured, who needs to prove it (the veteran or provider) and what happens if DVA determines that clinical need does not exist.

Jacqui Lambie has a question for male ministers This week Jacqui Lambie shared her health struggles while the government and Coalition were busy making deals and One Nation launched a debate about cigarettes.

But that has raised the concerns of veterans' advocate groups, many of whom are fiercely protesting the changes.

Llani Kennealy from Women Veterans Australia said setting the threshold at all sent the wrong message to veterans seeking care.

"Imposing the cap automatically makes the veteran community feel like we were doing something wrong, seeking treatment for conditions as a result of our service," she said.

And she argued it would have an immediate impact should it be introduced.

"I have concerns about people delaying care, not accessing care, worrying — not all veterans are capable or particularly in the mental state to go on MyGov and assess where they're at with their treatment," she said.

"So it has a huge impact on the veteran community, and quite frankly, it's just the government putting the burden on the veterans to go after the shonky operators that have been over-servicing the veteran community."

Under repeated questioning on the issue in parliament this week, the veterans affairs minister pointed to changes the government was making to try to improve access to allied health.

Phillip Thompson says the government's actions do not stack up to its words. (Supplied: Australian of the Year)

These include increasing fees paid to providers to try to encourage more to take on veterans as clients and removing requirements for referrals.

Mr Keogh said the government wanted its introduction to have as little real-world impact on veterans as possible.

"What we have always been very clear about … is that we would always ensure that there was continuity of access, and that we would engage with all of the veteran community in relation to how we made sure that we maintained that good access," he said.

The shadow minister for defence personnel, Phil Thompson, said the cap had to go.

"The Albanese Labor government talks about supporting veterans, but its actions tell a different story," said the former soldier, who served in Afghanistan.

"This cap puts access to vital treatment at risk for veterans dealing with physical injuries, mental health challenges and service-related trauma."

title: 'Horrific consequences': Aussie star almost hit by car in Tour of Britain
text:
Australian cyclist Maeve Plouffe has revealed she nearly got hit by a car while riding in this week's Tour of Britain — and has warned of potentially more "horrific consequences" for a sport already reeling from tragedy.

Plouffe, the 27-year-old former Sydney track star who grabbed Commonwealth team pursuit gold and individual silver in 2022, prompted organisers of the week-long road race to review safety procedures after she outlined her "scary" experience.

Plouffe had to withdraw from the race, having suffered a puncture during the opening stage in Cumbria on Wednesday, and her revelation on Instagram about an alarming episode with a car as she attempted to chase back to the peloton.

Plouffe posted the statement of her close call on her personal Instagram account. (Instagram/@maeveplouffe)

Her comments came only days after British rider Finlay Tarling died last week during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal after he was hit by a non-race light goods vehicle that had entered the course.

Explaining her withdrawal, Plouffe added: "While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.

"Later on, the moto escort was wonderful, and I felt much safer.

"But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."

She was referring to the death of the 19-year-old Tarling, who was killed last week in a high-speed collision with a van, which had strayed onto the road during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

British rider Finlay Tarling (right) was killed by a non-race light goods vehicle during the Volta a Portugal last week. (Getty Images: Huw Fairclough)

Before the Tour of Britain Women had begun, an emotional tribute was paid to Tarling, with his picture projected onto a large screen while all 114 riders and roadside fans joined in a minute's applause to honour him.

Tarling was the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who will ride the Vuelta a España Grand Tour, which begins on Saturday, in honour of his sibling.

Organisers have swiftly taken note of Plouffe with Jonathan Day, events director of British Cycling Ventures — the commercial arm of British Cycling that organises the Tour — saying in a statement: "We're taking those comments extremely seriously."

"Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.

"We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.

"We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how seriously we are treating these comments."

The race continued on Thursday with Dutch superstar Lorena Wiebes claiming her second successive stage victory between Clitheroe and Blackpool but only after that second stage had been neutralised because of a car accident.

Australian rider Georgia Baker, fresh from her golden Commonwealth Games on the track in Glasgow, was also caught up in a crash on the route.

Wiebes is 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Chiara Consonni (Canyon-SRAM zondacrypto) in the general classification as the race moves into Wales on Friday.

title: Live: Bitcoin surges on US policy signals, market down on plan to 'collapse' Iran's economy
text:
Last night on 'The Business' Martin Whetton from Westpac financial markets strategy team took apart the US bond market with Alicia Barry.

It's a great explainer.

Here are some of the key takeaway points:

"$85 billion a day the US government's paying its bondholders, its lenders, as is the technical term.

"And so that's obviously a lot, but it's not a lot relative to the size of how much debt they have. But that has jumped up pretty sharply from an average of around $20 billion two to three years ago.

"Now, as you say, the bond markets have been flashing red. What's been happening is there is a concern over inflation.

"There's a concern over lack of forward guidance from the Fed as to what they'll do on policy. There's an expectation of a rate hike, but there is still inflation and they're not combating that.

"There is quantitative tightening, so the central bank is reducing its holdings of government debt, so reducing its balance sheet.

"And then you've got the government itself borrowing money, plus you've got this new cohort of the hyperscalers who are around half a trillion dollars this year and about the same last year, whose credit ratings are extremely high, whose business models are very good.

"And they come at a yield over the government curve. And so investors who need to buy bonds for part of their superannuation portfolio or for regulatory reasons are saying, 'Well, I'd rather actually lend my money to Google or Meta or others rather than give it to the US government or in some countries, the sovereigns there'.

"And it's actually worth noting that yesterday Google or Alphabet was able to issue $5.5 billion Australian dollars in the market here. It's the largest ever corporate bond deal that we've seen by quite a margin.

"But the fact that it saw about $20 billion worth of orders suggests very, very high demand, again, for Australian dollars and the assets here, even though the company itself is not an Australian company."

title: Alcaraz confirms US Open return amid record prize money reveal
text:
Carlos Alcaraz is set to return to action at the US Open, ending four months of injury torment, and will be back competing for a record grand slam winner's prize of $US5.5 million ($7.7 million) in New York.

The news of the seven-time grand slam winner's comeback at Flushing Meadows will be music to the ears of former Australian Open boss Craig Tiley, who has been able to begin his reign in charge of the US Open by announcing unprecedented riches to the players.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz has not played since April due to a concerning wrist injury.

He announced his return on Thursday in unusual fashion, with the help of football journalist Fabrizio Romano.

Romano, who is usually breaking news of big football transfers, used his catchphrase, "Here we go," to announce Alcaraz's return on Instagram, while the reigning champ repeated the message on X.

Alcaraz, who started the year by winning the Australian Open, has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in April. He has missed both the ‌French Open and ⁠Wimbledon while his great rival, Jannik Sinner, has largely dominated.

Now he is fit to return to the scene of his first grand slam triumph in 2022, when he became the youngest man to reach world number one in the rankings.

Alcaraz's return is fantastic news for Tiley, the former Tennis Australia CEO who has taken up the equivalent job at the US Tennis Association (USTA) and has been able to announce an overall prize fund of $US108 million — the first time the $US100m barrier has been broken at a slam.

Alcaraz's 2026 season has been cruelled by a wrist injury. (Getty Images: Quality Sport Images/Alvaro Medranda)

It is the biggest prize pot in the sport's history and represents a 20 per cent rise for the second consecutive year.

"This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners," Tiley said.

"We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players."

That platform is the formation of a Grand Slam Player Council, which is intended to give players a voice on a range of issues such as prize money.

Organisers hope all this will ward off the kind of player protests that occurred at the French Open and Wimbledon.

The champions' winning cheque will be $US5.5 million, up from the $5 million that Sabalenka and Alcaraz won last year.

Players will earn $US140,000 just for making it into the main draw, while a quarterfinalist earns $US780,000, a semifinalist $US1.45 million and runners-up $US2.8 million.

Meanwhile, there was good news for the Australian challenge following the withdrawal of Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina from the main draw through injury.

It meant Alexei Popyrin was able to be advanced to the main draw and the reciprocal wildcard he had been given by the USTA could instead go to his Australian teammate Dane Sweeny, who will make his Flushing Meadows debut at 25.

That takes the current Australian contingent set to start the action on August 30 to a total of 14 — eight men and six women — with more attempting to make it through next week's qualifying.

AAP

title: Nicole Kidman’s third act has a disco beat. Shame the rest of us can’t keep up
text:

CultureCelebrityNicole Kidman Opinion Nicole Kidman’s third act has a disco beat. Shame the rest of us can’t keep up Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist August 21, 2026 — 11:30am

August 21, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When we met at the races back in 2012, Nicole Kidman was fun. Happy to yack away with a random on Derby Day, she kept pulling $100 notes from a little envelope and plonking them on the nose. I liked her panache. No pussyfooting around, just backing her instincts. Also, her heels were cracked like anyone’s are if they get around without shoes a lot. A weirdly cool move. A day at the races. Halfpenny (right) with Marie Claire editor Nicky Briger (left) and Nicole Kidman. I’ve cheered Nic on in her post-divorce life, the trips with her daughters, the way she looks in a tailored Chanel jean, her apparent refusal to stew on things. Smart PR move, positioning herself as the unbowed gal shucking off heartbreak to write her own third act at 59. But Nicole’s latest outing on the cover of UK Vogue has put me off a bit. Loved the styling – rugby jumper, sunnies on 1980s beauty queen hair – but inside, ah, Nic.

Advertisement

Her tales of what she’s been up to this northern summer, including hot nights in Ibiza, Spain, come close to what an early 2000s radio segment used to call Proclamations of a Wanker. “It’s a small dinner party or it’s a rave,” she said. “I’m either playing Scrabble or I’m out. It’s that simple.” The “out” version includes 10.30pm dinner and club at 1am, wearing glasses and sometimes “a little dark wig” so she can fly under the radar. Her clubbing cred was further boosted this week by her starring role in pop star Troye Sivan’s new video. Ibiza, it turns out, is just one stop. “I’m stealth,” said Nicole. “London, Ibiza, Paris, Portofino. A Euro summer.” Right. I don’t know what “I’m stealth” means, and I don’t know if all that makes me jealous or thrilled. Jealous because who wouldn’t want to teleport to that place and time? Hours on the D floor. Cultivating an air of mystery via a disguise. Getting trolleyed, staggering home thinking, “shit, Steps songs haven’t aged well” and “it’s true, bodysuits don’t need to be snapped up at the crotch”.

Advertisement

Our Nic rocks a rugby jumper on the cover of Vogue. Vogue/Instagram Thrilled because it’s lovely to see someone deciding, right, that last bit of my life was brutal, but I’m alive and I’m getting back out there. Most of us midlifers relish the idea of freedom from responsibilities other than making sure our wig’s still on. (PS Nicole, just saying, we would all still know it’s you, even with a kicky brunette pixie look.) But it’s not realistic. Start with the calendar. Nicole’s job requires her to turn up to a set for a couple of months, say words other people have written, emote, then leave with millions of dollars. The rest of us have the sort of work that wants us there on Monday. And Tuesday. And the Tuesday after that. There are kids to drive, dogs to walk, parents to help with online banking. Then there’s the money. Ibiza clubs surely mean a door price, a round or 40, a car home. Bloody expensive when you’re juggling school fees and car rego and mortgages.

Advertisement

The divorce bit is relevant to many of us, though, because that’s what this really is. A woman on the cusp of 60 feeling her way as a single person again, which is hard at any age. Losing the present and future you thought you’d have is devastating. It knocks confidence and destroys self-esteem. Makes you fear what comes next instead of seeing it as an opportunity. You wonder if you were ever loveable. Related Article Opinion

Royal family It’s obvious what’s behind Harry and Meghan’s return to Blighty. It’s not to reunite with Will and Kate Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist Nicole, good for her, may have already moved through that. She’s reportedly seeing a financier – lol – which does take some of the edge off any “brave lone wolf” narrative. Still. She could have gone quiet. She went dancing. That energy is something lots of us miss from a past life. Hands up anyone who can stay up all night – I need to know your secret. An achievable night out these days for me is a 5.45pm dinner, preferably around the corner, then home to spoon my dog once the electric blanket’s been on for a while.

Advertisement

So, is Nicole’s glamorous Euro summer ruining midlife for the rest of us? Nah. Is she giving post-divorce life a good name? I think so. She’s decided there’s still optimism to be found via bass lines shocking your heart into a new rhythm and thinking nothing can touch what freedom feels like for you. More power to you, disco lady. title: After two decades, China is preparing its boldest Moon mission yet
text:
In brief China's next moon mission is expected to launch later this month.

Chang'e 7's unique mission will try to find frozen water on the moon's surface and see if it could be accessed.

How do you explore a place where the sun never shines? China's space program will soon embark on one of the most innovative lunar exploration missions in recent years.

We’ve known for nearly two decades that some form of water exists on the moon. What we still don’t know is exactly how much accessible water ice lies inside permanently shadowed craters, how deeply it is buried or what form it takes.

What we do know is that accessing that water ice will be a real challenge: it is found at the bottom of deep, hard-to-traverse craters where the sun never shines, remaining untouched for billions of years at temperatures well below –200C. These are among the most valuable places on the moon, but the hardest to reach and explore.

Lunar exploration has come a long way since the Soviet Union’s Luna-1 probe reached the moon's vicinity in January 1959. The Apollo missions and their successors showed the challenge is no longer simply to reach the moon. It is to explore places human and conventional rovers cannot easily go, and ultimately determine whether the moon itself can provide some of the resources that future explorers will need.

China has spent two decades building an increasingly ambitious lunar exploration program, named after Chang'e, the ancient Chinese goddess of the moon. The Chang'e-7 mission is expected to set course for our celestial neighbour later this month, although a recent failure involving a different Chinese rocket has introduced some uncertainty over the launch date. Here’s what makes this latest mission so interesting.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is Chang'e-7 set to achieve?

The mission will test several novel approaches to lunar exploration. It will consist of an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper.

In addition, the Queqiao-2 lunar relay satellite is already in place. Launched separately in March 2024, it subsequently supported the Chang'e-6 mission and will facilitate communication between Earth and the lunar surface during the Chang'e-7 mission.

We don’t know precisely where the mission will land, but a site on or near an illuminated ridge close to the Shackleton crater in the Lunar South Pole’s Aitken region is a prime candidate.

The hopper will be the mission’s real star. Unlike a wheeled rover, it’s designed to leap over broken terrain and descend into craters where sunlight never reaches, places conventional vehicles may simply be unable to enter.

Adding it to the mission makes sense, given the steep crater walls, broken terrain, permanent shadow and the need for autonomous navigation and communications.

Chinese scientists won’t be looking for signs of water; we already have compelling evidence for lunar polar water. The question at the mission’s core is where exactly that water is located, in what form and concentration, and whether it could realistically be accessed.

This marks a transition from simply exploring the moon to determining whether its resources can actually be used.

How NASA is taking a different tack

Other nations are similarly interested in addressing that same question. The United States is pursuing the same longer-term objective of making sustained lunar operations possible. Although NASA will be confronted by the same physical problems, the American space agency has opted for a different solution.

Chang'e-7 is a coordinated state mission whose elements have been designed around a single, specific objective and which can use the already operational Queqiao-2 infrastructure.

NASA, by contrast, is deliberately trying something different: building a lunar marketplace through its Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme. The agency buys lunar delivery, mobility and technology services from companies that own and operate their own spacecraft.

NASA currently has 17 contracted deliveries carrying more than 60 instruments.

And the American effort has already yielded useful experience: Intuitive Machines’ IM-2 mission, Athena, attempted strikingly similar undertakings to Chang'e-7. It carried a drill and mass spectrometer looking for volatiles, a small hopping vehicle intended to explore difficult terrain and an experimental mobile communications network. However, the lander fell over at the landing site and was powered down just one day after arriving.

In essence, the destination dictates the problems; different space programmes are experimenting with different ways to resolve them.

Learning how to live on the moon

Finding lunar resources is only the first step. Chang'e-7 will attempt to determine where useful lunar resources are found near the moon's South Pole and characterise their nature.

Chang'e-8, slated for potential launch in 2028, will move towards demonstrating how they might actually be used.

Crewed exploration will likely follow, culminating in the construction of the International Lunar Research Station, jointly led by the China National Space Administration and Russia’s Roscosmos space agency.

On the other side of the Pacific, the CLPS will feed technology and science into the broader NASA-led Artemis program, which the agency explicitly describes as laying the foundation for sustained lunar exploration.

Ultimately, the lunar South Pole doesn’t care which flag is on a spacecraft. Any explorer entering its permanently shadowed craters faces the same darkness, severe cold, broken terrain and communications problems.

Getting to the moon was one of the great technological challenges of the 20th century. Learning how to live and work there may be one of the great challenges of the 21st.
